notes: One LSTM (one layer) is trained on all 12 basins together; the ten basin properties in flood.STATIC are repeated on every day as extra inputs. The baselines are one model per basin and lead.

Three of the ten basin properties (p_mean, aridity, p_seasonality: mean rain, dryness and rain season) are the CAMELS climate averages of October 1989 to September 2009 (stated in camels_attributes_v2.0.xlsx), a period that overlaps the validation years and four test years. Each is one fixed number per basin, not daily data, and no property comes from the flow record, but strictly they are not training-years-only information.

Hidden size is capped at 64 because of this laptop (2 CPU cores, no GPU); larger models were not tried. Only hidden size and learning rate were checked; dropout, history length, batch and training budget are the engine defaults.

Setting check: one seed per candidate, chosen by the mean validation-years NSE over the 12 basins and 3 leads (the score the trainer itself uses for early stopping). The chosen candidate leads the runner-up by 0.0052; the 3 seeds of the chosen setting differ by 0.0074 in the same score, so the choice is within seed noise: the candidates are practically equivalent and the pick is not a finding.

Training budget: at most 2000 updates, a validation check every 100, stop after 6 checks without a better score. 12 of the 14 trainings were stopped by that rule; 2 reached the update limit before the rule was met (past weather + perfect 3-day forecast, seed 0: best at update 1500; past weather + perfect 3-day forecast, seed 1: best at update 1800): a longer budget might have improved them.

Perfect weather forecast, LSTM against simple methods: like-for-like only at 3 days ahead (key like_for_like in the comparison). The LSTM reads the weather stamped on all three coming days at every lead; the simple methods of 02_baselines.py read it only up to the day being forecast. Because the rain table stamps rain by observer day (see 10_rain_timing.py), rain stamped one day after the target day still tells about the target day, so at 1 and 2 days ahead the LSTM knows more than the simple methods and no winner should be called there. The comparison of the LSTMs with each other (what the river gauge adds, what the weather of the coming days adds) is not affected.

Fair test: scalers, thresholds and weights use the training years 1980-2000 only; the setting, every stopping point and the 'best' baseline were chosen on the validation years 2000-2005; the test years 2005-2014 were scored only after all choices were made and chose nothing. The setting-check table holds no test score.

lstm_<set> is the day-by-day average of the forecasts of the seeds listed. An average of several models usually scores a little higher than each single one, so the per-seed medians (lstm_seed_median_min / max) and the basins won by each single seed (n_basins_lstm_higher_by_seed) are given next to every comparison. A baseline 'inside the seed spread' means that one training run of the LSTM could land on either side of it: read that as no clear difference.

Warnings of the seed average against its single seeds, over the 12 combinations of input set and lead (test years, onset warnings, pooled): its share of onsets warned is above every single seed in 7, inside their range in 5 and below every seed in 0; its share of false warnings is below every seed in 5, inside in 7 and above in 0. onset_pod_seed_min / max and onset_far_seed_min / max in decomposition.levels give the single-seed range next to the value of the seed average.
All models are compared on identical days: coverage is 1.0 for every model, lead and basin in the validation and test years (asserted in the code).

Wilcoxon signed-rank test, two-sided, over the 12 basins (LSTM seed average against the baseline). With 12 basins the smallest possible p is 0.0005; the basins are not independent (neighbours share storms) and many comparisons are made without correction, so read p as a description, not a proof.
median_nse_difference is the median over basins of (LSTM minus baseline); difference_of_medians is the median LSTM NSE minus the median baseline NSE. They need not agree.

Perfect weather forecast (wf, wqf) = the actual weather of the target days, an upper bound that cannot be had in practice. The comparison there is close but not exactly like-for-like: the LSTM reads all six weather variables of days t+1..t+3 at every lead, the baselines read rain and mean temperature of days t+1..t+k for lead k. At 3 days ahead both see the same days.

Skill decomposition: 'gain' = difference of the median test NSE of two LSTMs (seed averages) that differ in one source of information; nse_median_gain_seed_min / max repeat it seed by seed (seed s against seed s). clear_of_seed_noise is true when the per-seed medians of the two models do not overlap.

Warning scores are pooled over the 12 basins. High flow = above the basin's 95th percentile of the training years; onset = only forecasts issued while the river was still at or below that level. onset_far is the share of false warnings among the warnings issued in that situation.

lstm_all_scores.csv: test years, one row per basin, lead and model. gauge_id is text with a leading zero - read it with dtype=str. model is the name of the prediction set; inputs: w / wq / wf / wqf as in flood.INPUT_LABEL, q = river gauge only, calendar = no live data. pod, far, csi, hits, misses, false_alarms count all high-flow days; onset_pod and onset_far only the forecasts issued before the river was high. far is empty where a model gave no warning in that basin.

This file was written by --rescore: every score, table and note was recomputed from the saved prediction sets lstm_<set>_s<seed> without training again; the setting-check table, cost, training curves and the timings (n_trainings, training_seconds, waited_for_cpu_s, runtime_s) are those of the training run. rescore_runtime_s is the time of this pass.
